title: One complete original-paper proof reconstruction
subtitle: G2 lecture 129000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: The problem and its setting is the next step of the argument.
body: A Davis-Kahan perturbation proof combines several ingredients: spectral projections select invariant subspaces; residual identities generate Sylvester equations; a spectral gap bounds their solutions; principal-angle operators express the resulting geometry; and Ky Fan or pinching inequalities transfer block estimates to broader operator norms.

The argument must preserve each hypothesis through the chain. Our goal is to prove that delta times the unitarily invariant norm of the sine of the ambient angle is at most the norm of the perturbation.

slides.title: State the theorem precisely
slides.lead: Work first on a finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product space.
body: Let A and B be self-adjoint matrices, and write K for B minus A. Let U be a reducing subspace of A, and V a reducing subspace of B. Their projections are P and Q. Take a positive number delta. Assume the spectrum of A on U is separated from the spectrum of B on V perpendicular by at least delta in an interval-versus-exterior configuration. Assume also that the spectrum of B on V is similarly separated from the spectrum of A on U perpendicular by delta. These are two independent crossed separation conditions. They are stronger than saying each pair of selected eigenvalues is distinct.

slides.title: First prerequisite: a valid Sylvester inverse estimate
slides.lead: Consider a general equation H X minus X L equals C.
body: Suppose the spectrum of L lies in a closed interval from beta to alpha, while the spectrum of H lies outside the expanded open interval from beta minus delta to alpha plus delta. First handle the part of H's spectrum above alpha plus delta. Shift both operators by the same scalar alpha. On that high spectral component, H minus alpha is positive and at least delta, while L minus alpha is negative semidefinite. For positive time t, the product of the decaying exponential of minus t times H minus alpha, the operator C, and the exponential of t times L minus alpha has norm at most the norm of C times exponential of minus delta t.

slides.title: Build the first crossed equation
slides.lead: Define X as the cross projection from U into V perpendicular.
body: Because U reduces A and V perpendicular reduces B, the restricted operators compose with X in the expected way. Compute B on V perpendicular times X, minus X times A on U. The two terms combine into the V-perpendicular projection of B minus A applied to U. In other words, the Sylvester right-hand side is the corresponding block of K. The first separation hypothesis therefore yields, for every positive integer k, delta times the first k singular values of X added together at most the first k singular values of that K block added together.

slides.title: Build the reverse crossed equation
slides.lead: Now define X prime as the cross projection from U perpendicular into V.
body: This is the adjoint of the escape map from V into U perpendicular, so it has the same nonzero singular values as that reverse escape. Compute B on V times X prime, minus X prime times A on U perpendicular. The resulting right-hand side is the other selected block of K. The second separation hypothesis gives the same all-prefix inequality for X prime and that second K block. This step is the reason Proposition six point one is symmetric. A single trial residual would give only one equation; our two reducing subspaces and ambient perturbation give a matched pair.

slides.title: Identify the ambient angle algebraically
slides.lead: Let D be P minus Q.
body: Expand D squared. Since P and Q are orthogonal projections, D squared equals P plus Q minus P Q minus Q P. On the decomposition U plus U perpendicular, this operator is block diagonal. On U, its block is the cross projection X adjoint X. On U perpendicular, its block is the product of the adjoint of X prime with X prime. Taking the positive square root gives the modulus of D. Its nonzero singular values are exactly those of X together with those of X prime, including multiplicities. This is the exact ambient sine representation. If U and V have unequal dimensions, right-angle defect directions are included in the appropriate cross block.

slides.title: Prove the direct-sum prefix step
slides.lead: For any two matrices M and N, the sum of the largest k singular values of their orthogonal direct sum is the maximum over all splits of k into i and k minus i, of the first i singular values of M plus the first k minus i of N.
body: Why? The singular values of the direct sum are the decreasing rearrangement of the two component lists. Choosing the top k entries is equivalent to choosing some number from the first list and the remaining number from the second. The best such split gives exactly the prefix sum. Apply this identity to X and X prime.

slides.title: Prove the pinching step
slides.lead: The pair of right-hand-side K blocks occupies orthogonal input and output corners, after reordering the output decomposition V plus V perpendicular.
body: Call their block sum K pinched. Construct an input reflection that is positive on U and negative on U perpendicular. Construct an output reflection with opposite signs on V and V perpendicular, chosen so the selected corners keep their sign. Conjugating K by the output reflection on the left and input reflection on the right negates the discarded corners and preserves the selected corners. Average this transformed operator with K. The off-diagonal corners cancel, leaving K pinched. Both reflections are unitary.

slides.title: Put the inequalities together
body: First, the two crossed Sylvester equations yield the respective delta-scaled bounds. Second, direct-sum comparison combines them into an ambient sine prefix inequality. Third, pinching bounds the combined perturbation blocks by the original K at every prefix. Thus, for each k, delta times the Ky Fan k norm of the ambient sine is at most the Ky Fan k norm of K. In finite dimensions every unitarily invariant norm is determined by a symmetric gauge of the singular values. A weak-majorization inequality for all prefixes implies the corresponding symmetric-gauge inequality. Consequently delta times N of the ambient sine is at most N of K.

slides.title: Extend the logic to Hilbert-space ideals
slides.lead: The original source works in a separable Hilbert space.
body: Here an arbitrary bounded operator need not have finite N norm, and singular-value prefixes are formulated using approximation numbers. The bounded self-adjoint restrictions and crossed interval-versus-exterior gaps still supply the corresponding Sylvester estimates. The reflection identity is algebraic, hence valid on Hilbert spaces. The direct-sum prefix principle uses approximation-number machinery rather than a finite list of matrix singular values. To avoid assuming the conclusion's finiteness, begin with K in the chosen symmetric ideal.

slides.title: One sharp example and one boundary failure
slides.lead: Take A with eigenvalues zero and four, and let B be its rotation by theta.
body: Choose U and V as the corresponding zero-eigenspaces. Both crossed gaps are four. The operator norm of their projection difference is sine theta, while the norm of B minus A is four sine theta. Equality holds. Now imagine using only the first crossed equation and allowing U to be a line contained in a larger V. Its directed sine is zero, while the ambient projection difference has norm one. Without the second equation, the ambient conclusion cannot follow. This checks the logic of the theorem, not just its numerical constant.

slides.title: Final reconstruction
slides.lead: The proof rests on four mathematical mechanisms that now have independent justifications.
body: Self-adjoint spectral restrictions and crossed gaps authorize two Sylvester inverses. Projection algebra identifies the ambient sine with two directed singular-value lists. Ky Fan direct-sum comparison merges the two spectral estimates. Reflection averaging contracts the pair of perturbation blocks into the original perturbation. Tracking ideal membership makes the argument valid beyond matrices. Tracking both gap conditions prevents a directed theorem from being misstated as an ambient one.

slides.title: What to retain
slides.lead: Together, the domain conditions, the two gap assumptions, the Sylvester estimate, and the singular-value comparison establish Proposition six point one.
